mainTopic: Who must bring proof in sale and חזקה disputes: the בר סיסין field, the owner who was away in the markets, and a purchase through a middleman.
overview: A man sold 'all the property of בי בר סיסין', then said one field was only called by that name and was not part of the sale. רב נחמן gave the field to the buyer, but רבא objected: המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, so the one trying to take must bring proof. The גמרא notes that in the earlier case of the owner who said he was far away, each of them seemed to rule the other way. For רבא, the answer is that he always favors whoever holds the land: here the seller, there the buyer. For רב נחמן, the seller's own wording puts the burden on him here, while there the buyer's חזקה is like a שטר that must first be confirmed. Next comes a house dispute: the owner says he was away in far-off markets, and the one living there brings witnesses that he came home for thirty days every year. רבא accepts the owner's answer that a person can be busy in the market for all thirty days. A new land case then begins, where the possessor says he bought through a middleman, and the owner's reply continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The case of the בר סיסין field
steps.stepSummary: A seller sold 'all the property of בי בר סיסין' and then claimed one field bearing that name was not included.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man told his friend: I am selling you all the property of בי בר סיסין. There was one field that people called 'of בי בר סיסין'. The seller said: this field is not really from בי בר סיסין; it is only called that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story to set up a ruling about who has to bring proof. Here we only hear the facts of the dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sale was described by a name, 'property of בי בר סיסין'. One field carries that name, but the seller says the name is just a nickname, not a sign of where the land really came from. So the question is whether this field was part of the sale.

phrases.english: who said to his fellow:
phrases.notes: The story actually starts on the previous page with 'ההוא', meaning 'a certain man', so read it as 'a certain man who said...'.

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל נִכְסֵי דְּבֵי בַּר סִיסִין – מְזַבֵּינָא לָךְ.
phrases.english: All the property of the house of bar Sisin, I am selling to you.
There was a certain piece of land
that was called 'of the house of bar Sisin.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָא לָאו דְּבֵי בַּר סִיסִין הִיא,
phrases.english: He said to him: This one is not really of the house of bar Sisin,
phrases.notes: The seller is the one speaking here, to the buyer.

phrases.english: it is merely called 'of the house of bar Sisin.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: כׇּל נִכְסֵי דְּבֵי בַּר סִיסִין – מְזַבֵּינָא לָךְ
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the facts: a seller claims a field called 'בי בר סיסין' was not really included in the sale.

steps.title: רב נחמן gives the field to the buyer
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that the field belongs to the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came before רב נחמן, and he left the field in the hands of the buyer.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן decides the case: the buyer gets the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the seller still holds the land, רב נחמן treats the name of the field as enough to put it into the sale. The buyer wins unless the seller proves otherwise.

keyTerms.meaning: he established it, he left it

phrases.english: They came before Rav Nachman,
he established it in the hands of the buyer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן, אוֹקְמָא בִּידָא דְלוֹקֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the case just described.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The field goes to the buyer.

steps.title: רבא objects: the one taking must bring proof
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רב נחמן using the rule המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Is that the law?! The one who wants to take from his fellow must bring the proof!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's ruling as going against a basic rule of monetary law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller is the one holding the field now. The buyer wants to take it away from him, so by the standard rule the buyer should have to prove the field was included. Without that proof, the land should stay with the seller.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this the law?! (a sharp challenge)
The one who wants to take from another must bring proof

phrases.english: Rava said to him: Is this the law?!
The one who takes from his fellow, the proof is upon him!

steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling for the buyer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The seller is in possession, so the buyer is the one taking and should need proof.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the contradictions that follow, because in the earlier case each אמורא seemed to say the opposite.

steps.title: Each sage seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that רבא and רב נחמן each seem to contradict what they said in the earlier case.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a contradiction between רבא and רבא, and a contradiction between רב נחמן and רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא compares this story to the earlier case where someone said he had been far away. There, each sage seemed to rule the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case, רב נחמן ruled for the original owner, the one who said he had been far away, against the buyer living in the house. There רבא ruled for the buyer. Here it is the reverse: רב נחמן rules for the buyer, and רבא rules for the seller. So each one seems to switch sides between seller and buyer.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not get mixed up: 'contradiction of רבא against רבא' means רבא against himself, comparing this case with the earlier one. It is not רבא against רב נחמן.

phrases.english: There is a difficulty of Rava against Rava,
phrases.notes: Compare this with the earlier case on the previous page, about the man who said he had been far away.

phrases.english: there is a difficulty of Rav Nachman against Rav Nachman.

steps.triggerLanguage: קַשְׁיָא דְּרָבָא אַדְּרָבָא, קַשְׁיָא דְּרַב נַחְמָן אַדְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares steps 2 and 3 with the earlier case and finds internal contradictions.
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of both רבא and רב נחמן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the earlier case רב נחמן favored the seller and רבא the buyer; here רב נחמן favors the buyer and רבא the seller.

steps.title: רבא is consistent: it depends on who holds the land
steps.stepSummary: רבא always favors whoever is in possession. Here that is the seller; in the earlier case it was the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא against רבא is not a problem. There, the seller is the one holding his property; here, the buyer is the one holding the property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction in רבא: he follows one rule in both cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's single principle is המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה. In the בר סיסין case the seller still holds the land, so the buyer must prove. In the earlier case the buyer was living in the house, so the other side must prove.

phrases.english: Rava against Rava is not difficult:
there, the seller stands in his property,
phrases.notes: 'There' means our case, the בר סיסין field.

phrases.english: here, the buyer stands in the property.
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the earlier case, where the buyer was living in the house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by who is in possession
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא favors the seller in one case and the buyer in the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא always favors the one in possession; possession just differed between the cases.

steps.title: רב נחמן is consistent: the wording and the 'document' idea
steps.stepSummary: Here the seller's own words put the burden on him. In the earlier case, a חזקה is like a שטר, which must be confirmed before it helps.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן against רב נחמן is also not a problem. Since the seller said 'property of בי בר סיסין', and this field is called 'בי בר סיסין', it is on him to show it is not really from there. But in the earlier case, it is no better than if the possessor were holding a document. Wouldn't we tell him: confirm your document, and then you can stay in the property?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction in רב נחמן by showing that each case has its own reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the בר סיסין case the field matches the name the seller used, so he is the one who must prove it was excluded. In the earlier case the possessor relied on his years of living there, a חזקה, which takes the place of a שטר. Just as a שטר must be confirmed through witnesses before it helps, his חזקה must first be clarified, so the claimant wins.

keyTerms.meaning: it is placed upon him (the burden is his)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא: whoever is in possession wins unless the other side proves. רב נחמן: if the seller's own words point to the field, he must prove it was excluded. But a חזקה works like a שטר, and must be confirmed before it can protect the one living in the property.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַב נַחְמָן אַדְּרַב נַחְמָן נָמֵי לָא קַשְׁיָא –
phrases.english: Rav Nachman against Rav Nachman is also not difficult:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: דְּבֵי בַּר סִיסִין,
phrases.english: since he said to him 'of the house of bar Sisin,'
and it is called 'of the house of bar Sisin,'
it is upon him to reveal
that it is not of the house of bar Sisin.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, לֹא יְהֵא אֶלָּא דְּנָקֵיט שְׁטָרָא –
phrases.english: But here, let it be no better than if he were holding a document:
phrases.notes: The one living in the house relies on his years there, so treat that like holding a deed.

phrases.english: wouldn't we say to him:
Confirm your document, and then stand in the property?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַב נַחְמָן אַדְּרַב נַחְמָן נָמֵי לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second half of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by the reason behind each ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן favors the seller (original owner) in the earlier case and the buyer in the בר סיסין case, with no consistent logic.
steps.terutzMaskana: Here the seller's own wording places the burden on him. There, a חזקה is like a שטר and must first be confirmed.

steps.title: A house dispute: the owner claims he was far away
steps.stepSummary: A man claims a house. The one living there says he bought it and has a חזקה. The claimant answers that he was away in distant markets.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone said to another: Why are you in this house? He answered: I bought it from you, and I have lived in it for the years needed for a חזקה. The first one said: I was away in the far-off markets.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story and sets out both sides' claims. This sets up the back-and-forth that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually, living in a property for the years of חזקה proves you bought it, because the owner would have protested. The claimant attacks that logic: he was far away, so he never knew he had to protest. If that is true, the years of living there prove nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The years of use (three years) that prove ownership

phrases.english: There was a certain person who said to another:
What are you doing in this house?
He said to him: I bought it from you,
and I used it for the years of חזקה.
He said to him: I was in the outer marketplaces.
phrases.notes: He means he was too far away to know someone was living in his house, so he couldn't protest.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: מַאי בָּעֵית בְּהַאי בֵּיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about חזקה, separate from the field case discussed in steps 2-6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is set up: the possessor claims a purchase plus חזקה, and the claimant claims he was away and could not protest.

steps.title: The possessor brings witnesses that the owner came home every year
steps.stepSummary: The possessor says he has witnesses that the claimant came back for thirty days each year, so he could have protested.
steps.simpleTranslation: The possessor said: But I have witnesses that every year you came here for thirty days!
steps.whatsHappening: The possessor pushes back against the claimant's excuse. If the claimant was home every year, he could have found out and protested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The excuse 'I was far away' only works if he really had no chance to know. Witnesses showing he came back every year seem to cancel that excuse.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְהָא אִית לִי סָהֲדִי
phrases.english: He said to him: But I have witnesses

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֹל שַׁתָּא הֲוָה אָתֵית תְּלָתִין יוֹמֵי!
phrases.english: that every year you would come here for thirty days!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claimant's excuse from step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claimant's excuse that he was away in distant markets.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he came back for thirty days every year, he had a chance to learn about the possessor and protest, so his silence should count against him.

steps.title: The owner answers: I was busy those thirty days
steps.stepSummary: The claimant says that during those thirty days he was busy with his business in the market.
steps.simpleTranslation: The claimant said: During those thirty days I was busy in my markets.
steps.whatsHappening: The claimant defends his excuse. Even when he was in town, he was too busy with business to notice and protest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny that he came back. He says that coming back is not the same as having real time to deal with his property.

phrases.english: He said to him: Those thirty days,
I was busy in my marketplaces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the witnesses brought in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the facts but gives them a new meaning.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Coming home for thirty days a year means he could have protested.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was busy with business the whole time, so he had no real chance to protest.

steps.title: רבא accepts the owner's excuse
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a person can really be busy in the market for all thirty days, so the claimant's excuse is believable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is normal for a person to be busy in the market for the whole thirty days.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא decides the case. He accepts the claimant's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since a person can be busy the whole visit, the yearly thirty days did not give him a real chance to protest. So the possessor's years of use do not count as a חזקה here, and the house goes back to the claimant.

keyTerms.meaning: A person tends to, it is normal for a person

steps.whatToRemember: A חזקה only works if the owner had a real chance to protest. Being in town but busy with business for thirty days does not count as a real chance.

phrases.english: Rava said:
A person is apt, for all thirty days,
to be busy in the market.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the dispute in favor of the claimant's answer in step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The claimant's excuse stands. Thirty days of being busy in the market is not a real chance to protest, so the possessor has no חזקה.

steps.title: A land dispute: the possessor bought it through a middleman
steps.stepSummary: A new case. The possessor says he bought the land from a third person, who told him he had bought it from the claimant.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone said to another: Why are you on this land? He answered: I bought it from so-and-so, who told me he bought it from you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a second story and sets out the possessor's claim. This sets up the claimant's answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the possessor does not say he bought it from the claimant directly. He says it came to him through a middleman, and he only knows about the first sale because the middleman told him.

phrases.english: There was a certain person who said to another:
What are you doing on this land?
He said to him: I bought it from so-and-so,
who told me that he bought it from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: מַאי בָּעֵית בְּהַאי אַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, separate story after רבא's ruling in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is set up: the possessor claims he bought the land through a middleman who said he bought it from the claimant.

steps.title: The owner starts to push back
steps.stepSummary: The claimant begins his answer: 'Don't you admit...'. The rest of his sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: The claimant said: Don't you admit...
steps.whatsHappening: The claimant starts to attack the possessor's claim. His full point finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claimant is about to use the possessor's own words against him. The possessor never said he bought the land from the claimant himself, so the claimant is pointing at something the possessor has already admitted.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַתְּ לָאו קָא מוֹדֵית
phrases.english: He said to him: Don't you admit
phrases.notes: His sentence isn't finished yet. It continues on the next page, where he says what the possessor admits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The claimant answers the possessor's claim from step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possessor's claim that he bought the land through a middleman.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The claimant starts to use the possessor's own admission against him. The full argument continues on the next amud.
